subject: defining autodiffable functions with function classes

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: defining autodiffable functions with function classes
parts:
I just pushed a branch feature/functor, which allows
you to define a fairly simply functor and get all
of the autodiff behavior without having to worry about
autodiff types. It's only a few files and the tests
have some examples.

To define a unary function for fvar<double> and var,
this is enough:


// f(x) = exp(x)
// dx(x,f(x)) = d/dx f(x)
class exp_fun {
public:
static inline double f(double x) {
return std::exp(x);
}
static inline double dx(double /*x*/, double fx) {
return fx;
}
};

template <typename T>
inline T my_exp(const T& x) {
using stan::math::apply;
return apply<exp_fun>(x);
}

The thing to note here is that the class exp_fun is all static, and
is really just be using to give a name to the functions f() and dx().
The dx() function takes both the input and the function value. Here,
the input isn't used because d/dx exp(x) = exp(x).
I did this because derivatives often involve the result as a term.

Alternative 1: save the partial as in OperandsAndPartials; this takes
more space and really is behind the scenes for the way the functions
are defined.

Alternative 2: require f_dx(double x, double& dx); this is complicated
in higher-order settings, though, where we require x and dx to be
templated. The benefit is that it allows maximal sharing in the
computation of fx and its derivatives. It also doesn't allow an
efficient version of computing just the function itself, which isn't
good for a library.

Alternative 3: Should I use "operator()" instead of "f" to make the
function classes exp_fun and hypot_fun functors in the strict C++ sense?
(The apply class itself is defined as a functor to simplify the syntax.)

A binary function looks like this:

struct hypot_fun {
static inline double f(double x1, double x2) {
return std::sqrt(x1 * x1 + x2 * x2);
}
static inline double dx1(double x1, double /*x2*/, double fx) {
return x1 / fx;
}
static inline double dx2(double /*x1*/, double x2, double fx) {
return x2 / fx;
}
};

template <typename T1, typename T2>
inline typename boost::math::tools::promote_args<T1,T2>::type
my_hypot(const T1& x1, const T2&x2) {
using stan::math::apply;
return apply<hypot_fun>(x1,x2);
}

I wanted to run the general pattern by people before going on.

It's easy to define vectorized versions of these functions elementwise.
Just a few more definitions for the apply functor.

All the fiddling about is static and inlined, so it should be efficient.

In order to define a function that also applies to fvar<var>,
fvar<fvar<double> >, and fvar<fvar<var> >, the derivative functions
dx, dx1, and dx2 need to be templated out and those templates need to
be instanitatiable with var, fvar<double> and fvar<var> respectively.
There are examples in the tests for fwd mode auto-diff. Unfortunately,
that then requires a lot of testing of the function classes like my_hypot
to make sure they can apply to the correct types. We might be able to
automate this like the distribution tests.

- Bob

On Tuesday, July 9, 2013 5:03:23 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Alternative 3: Should I use "operator()" instead of "f" to make the
function classes exp_fun and hypot_fun functors in the strict C++ sense?
(The apply class itself is defined as a functor to simplify the syntax.)

If you make them genuine functors, you can call them elementwise on an Eigen::Array.

Just search for functor on

http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox-devel/classEigen_1_1Array.html

Ben
